newsitem.title: USA: Test measures risk of death to heart attack victims.
newsitem.headline: Test measures risk of death to heart attack victims.

text.p: A blood test which measures chemicals released from a damaged heart helps gauge the chance of death among patients with a suspected heart attack, two teams of medical researchers have found.
In tests on hundreds of patients suffering from chest pains, doctors found that when levels of the two chemicals, called troponin, were elevated, so was the risk of death.
But the troponin tests are far from a perfect predictor of who is likely to die, according to two studies published in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine.
In the study of 801 patients led by Dr. Magnus Ohman of Duke University, 289 had high levels of troponin T. Although 12 percent died within 30 days, 88 percent survived.
The second team, headed by Dr. Elliott Antman of Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston, looked at a different group of heart patients using another kind of troponin known as troponin I.
In their study, the team found a death rate of nearly four percent when the troponin I levels were high, compared with one percent when the chemical was hard to find in the blood.
Both groups found that the more troponin in the blood, the greater the risk.

Although the blood test missed more than seven out of eight deaths, the researcher said it should be a welcome addition to the imperfect arsenal of tests doctors use to try to pick out patients who face the greatest threat of death a month or so after a heart attack.
The troponin T test, which costs about $30, is made by the German pharmaceutical company Boehringer Mannheim. It was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 1994.

The troponin I test, which has been on the market since August 1995, is manufactured by Dade International, which paid for the Antman study. It is touted as a better indicator when it's used to diagnose a heart attack because of its speed. Results are available in about 10 minutes compared to the troponin T test, which takes as long as 45 minutes.

The traditional tests for assessing a possible heart attack involve measuring the electrical activity of the heart (an EKG) and looking for a chemical, creatine kinase, that is released when heart muscle (and other muscle) is damaged.
The Ohman team found that their troponin test was more accurate than an EKG or the creatine kinase test.

In an editorial in the New England Journal of Medicine, Dr. Frans Van de Werf of Gasthuisberg University in Leuven, Belgium, said it "is very likely" that a troponin test "will provide a more sensitive and specific indication of those at increased risk for cardiac events, including deaths."
